fields.meta_title: Fragrance Quiz Builder for Shops and Scent Brands | Emergent
fields.meta_description: Take the fragrance quiz to find your scent family, then build your own for a perfume shop, candle stall, or sample subscription.
fields.h1: Build a Fragrance Quiz That Sells the Matching Scent
fields.hero_description: Take the fragrance quiz below to find your scent family, or build one for your shop that keeps every answer in a database you own.
fields.features_heading: The Working Parts of a Fragrance Quiz
fields.features_subheading: Emergent builds the quiz and the database behind it, and a follow-up prompt changes either one before launch.
fields.feature_1:
Questions mapped to scent families

Name the families your quiz sorts people into, such as Floral or Woody. Emergent builds the questions with every option tied to one family and rewords any of them by prompt.
fields.feature_2:
Result pages that show tagged products

Each result page lists the bottles or candles you tagged with that family, pulled from your catalog. A Woody result ends on something a shopper can put straight in the cart.
fields.feature_3:
Answers kept in a database you own

Each finish lands as a row holding the family, every option picked, and the email if one was given. Filter rows by family to see which scents your visitors lean toward over time.
fields.feature_4:
Follow-up email sorted by family

The app passes each result and email to any tool with an API, so a welcome flow can open with sandalwood for Woody and citrus for Fresh instead of one message for everyone.
fields.feature_5:
A phone flow with no response caps

People answer one question per screen on a phone, at a market stall or from an email. Emergent puts no cap on responses, so a busy market weekend never cuts the quiz off early.
fields.feature_6:
Code you can take with you

Host the quiz on a custom domain, included in Emergent and billed in credits. On paid plans, export the full code to your GitHub repository and run the quiz anywhere you choose.

fields.usecase_heading: What Four Shops Do With a Fragrance Quiz
fields.tab_content_1:
Three tagged bottles and one discovery set

Romy Sarto finishes the fragrance quiz on Averill Scent Co.'s site and lands on Woody. The result page shows the 3 bottles tagged Woody and an $18 discovery set of all 3, pulled from the store catalog. Her family and email are saved to Averill's customer table, and the next email she gets opens with sandalwood.
fields.tab_content_2:
Every first box follows its quiz result

Vireo Sample Club puts the quiz in front of every new subscriber before the first box ships. Results group the packing list by scent family, and the warehouse pulls one shelf at a time. In March, 76 of 214 new boxes landed on Fresh and took the citrus samples in a single pass.
fields.tab_content_3:
Shoppers who land on Amber get a code

A QR code on Hearthwick's market stall opens the fragrance quiz on shoppers' phones. Anyone who lands on Amber sees the code AMBER10, good for 10% off the amber candle line through Sunday. By close, 14 shoppers had redeemed it, each redemption tied to the quiz answers that earned it.
fields.tab_content_4:
One season of quizzes, one spring brief

Solenne reads a season of quiz results before its spring launch. Of 1,240 finishes, Floral leads with 430 and Amber trails at 180, with Fresh at 360 and Woody at 270. The founder briefs the perfumer around a floral opener and moves the planned amber release to fall.

fields.howto_title: How to Make a Fragrance Quiz
fields.howto_description: Plan a fragrance quiz in seven steps, from the families it names to what each result sells, then build it with Emergent.
fields.howto_step_1_title: 01 Choose what a result should name
fields.howto_step_3_title: 03 Map every option to one family
fields.howto_step_4_title: 04 Give each result page a next step
fields.howto_step_1_des: Decide whether the quiz ends on a scent family or a single product. Families such as Floral or Woody stay stable as the catalog turns over, and a result page keeps its link while the bottles behind it change. Put that choice in your prompt.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Write questions around things people already know: their coffee order or the jacket they reach for on a cold morning. A shopper who cannot name a single note can still answer every one, and each option still points at one family.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Matching quizzes score by count: whichever family collects the most picks becomes the result. Give every option exactly one family, spread each family across several questions, and decide up front which result wins a tie so the same answers always land in the same place.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Name the family, describe it in a sentence or two, then show what to do about it: the tagged bottles, a sample set, or a code. A result page that ends with nothing to click ends the visit with it.
fields.howto_step_5_title: 05 Ask for the email after the result
fields.howto_step_5_des: Show the result first, then offer to send it along with a code or a sample offer. Keep the field optional. Answers tied to an address are worth more than an address alone, because the follow-up can lead with the right family.
fields.howto_step_6_title: 06 Run a test group before launch
fields.howto_step_6_des: Send the quiz to 10 people whose tastes you know and read where they land. When one family never comes up, reword one or two of its options instead of adding questions, and check that a tie still lands where you want it.
fields.howto_step_7_title: 07 Put the quiz where buyers already are
fields.howto_step_7_des: Link it from product pages and print a QR code for the stall or the counter. Then watch the family counts in the database: they tell you what to stock more of, and what the next launch should lead with.

faq_plan.a: A fragrance quiz is a short set of preference questions that sorts the person taking it into a scent family or toward a specific perfume. On a shop's site it works as a product finder: each option points at a family, the family picked most often wins, and the result page recommends matching bottles or samples.

faq_plan.q: How do I create a fragrance quiz?
faq_plan.a: Describe it in one prompt to Emergent's AI survey builder: the families you want, the questions, and what each result page shows. Emergent builds the quiz, the result pages, and the database the answers land in, and a follow-up prompt changes any of them before you share the link.

faq_plan.q: Is there a free fragrance quiz I can put on my own site?
faq_plan.a: Yes. A free fragrance quiz can run on Emergent's free tier, which covers building and publishing. Emergent also puts no response caps on it: a newsletter feature or a busy market weekend never shuts the quiz off.

faq_plan.q: What fragrance quiz questions work for shoppers who do not know perfume terms?
faq_plan.a: Ask about the familiar, not the technical: a Saturday outfit or the candle someone lights at home. Options like a lake cabin or a spice market each map cleanly to one family. If the quiz opens a quiz funnel that ends on a product page, put the easiest question first and save anything personal for the end.

faq_plan.q: How many questions should a fragrance quiz have?
faq_plan.a: Keep it between 6 and 10. That is enough for each family to be picked more than once and short enough to finish standing at a market stall. If you want more nuance, add detail to the result pages instead of adding questions; the quiz earns the result, and the result does the explaining.

faq_plan.q: How does a fragrance quiz turn answers into a scent family?
faq_plan.a: Each option carries one scent family, and the quiz counts them: the family picked most often is the result, with ties going to the one you rank first. Nothing is weighted behind the scenes, and two Woody picks beat one of everything else.

faq_plan.q: Can a fragrance quiz segment my email list by scent preference?
faq_plan.a: Yes. Each finish saves the family beside the email, which splits the list into segments the first time someone answers. A welcome flow can lead with woods for one subscriber and citrus for another. A marketing quiz builds segments the same way; the fragrance version names them after scents.

faq_plan.q: Can a fragrance quiz pull recommendations from my existing product catalog?
faq_plan.a: It can. The app connects to a catalog that has an API and syncs the products you tag with each family, and the result page lists whichever of them are in stock. Tag products once and the quiz stays current as inventory moves; nothing on the result page is maintained by hand.

faq_plan.q: Can I see which fragrance quiz answers produced each scent family result?
faq_plan.a: Yes. Emergent builds the quiz with a response table you own, and every finish lands there as a row: the final family next to every option picked on the way there. Read the rows when a result feels off. If Woody wins far more than it should, they show which question tips it, and you reword one option instead of rebuilding the quiz.

faq_plan.q: Does the matching pattern behind a fragrance quiz work for other product finders?
faq_plan.a: It does. The matching logic is not fragrance-specific: options carry a result, and the highest count wins. A gym matching people to training styles builds a fitness quiz the same way, and a bookshop can match readers to shelves. Swap the families for programs or genres and keep the scoring.

quiz.title: Which Fragrance Family Is Yours?
quiz.intro: Eight questions about the things you already like. Your answers point to one of four scent families: Floral, Fresh, Woody, or Amber.

questions.text: Where would you spend a free Saturday afternoon?

options.text: A garden market with armfuls of cut flowers
A beach walk with the wind coming off the water
A forest trail after a night of rain
A spice market with tea brewing at every stall

questions.text: What do you order at a coffee shop?

options.text: A lavender or rose latte
An iced tea with lemon
A plain black coffee, dark roast
A chai or a vanilla latte

questions.text: Pick a candle for your living room.

options.text: Peony and jasmine
Sea salt and cucumber
Cedar and smoke
Vanilla and cinnamon

questions.text: Which season do you look forward to most?

options.text: Spring, when everything is in bloom
Summer, with the windows open
Fall, with leaves underfoot
Winter, by a warm fire

questions.text: Which fabric would you wear all day if you could?

options.text: Soft silk in a pale print
Crisp white cotton
Worn-in flannel or suede
Heavy cashmere in a deep color

questions.text: What dessert do you reach for first?

options.text: A raspberry and rose macaron
Lemon sorbet
A walnut and maple tart
Salted caramel with a pinch of cardamom

questions.text: When should a scent be noticed?

options.text: When someone leans in for a hug
Right after a shower, then it fades
Close to the skin, almost private
Across the room, lingering after you leave

questions.text: Pick a place to stay for a weekend away.

options.text: A cottage with a rose garden
A white room overlooking the sea
A cabin in the pines
A riad with lanterns and low cushions

results.title: Floral
results.description: Your answers lean toward petals and soft sweetness. Start with rose, jasmine, peony, or orange blossom, and try a fruity floral if you want something brighter for daytime.

results.title: Fresh
results.description: Your answers lean toward clean, bright, and airy. Start with citrus like bergamot or grapefruit, green notes like cut grass, or sea salt, and keep a spray in your bag for a midday refresh.

results.title: Woody
results.description: Your answers lean toward quiet depth. Start with cedar, sandalwood, or vetiver, and look for a touch of leather or smoke when you want something for the evening.

results.title: Amber
results.description: Your answers lean toward warm and rich. Start with vanilla, resin, or spices like cardamom and cinnamon, and save the heaviest bottles for cold weather and nights out.

Every finish lands in a database the owner keeps.
